body.text: At the end of the Shrikant Verma Shikhar Samman ceremony, Abhishek Verma, on behalf of the Shrikant Verma Trust, said that literature should be kept completely separate from politics. Anca Verma, speaking on behalf of the Trust, elaborated on his statement: “Literature and politics should always be kept separate. He said that today there are very few people who are genuinely committed to the welfare of writers, and that there is an urgent need to protect, nurture, and encourage literature and writers. He also expressed concern that sincere efforts made for the advancement of literature are sometimes viewed through the prism of politics, criticism, and personal animosity, ultimately causing harm to literature itself. He said that the Shrikant Verma Trust would continue to uphold these values concerning the rights of literature and writers with conviction and dedication.”

I do not know how many of the writers and artists sitting on the stage, or those present in the auditorium, paused to think about this statement. What does literature need protection from? What does the welfare of writers mean? If we understand protection in economic terms, then why talk only of writers? Workers, farmers, teachers—everyone needs economic security. A writer does not place herself in some special category. Not even the writer who lives merely by the pen. And no award can meet a writer’s economic needs. What writers actually need is fair remuneration for the labour of writing. That is something no writer in India gets.

A writer does not need protection. Or patronage. A writer needs freedom. Freedom of expression. This is the first right of a writer, as it is of every other person, though for a writer it is perhaps even more fundamental. And freedom is the first value that literature itself proposes.
A trust, a party, a contradiction

There was a considerable irony in the fact that the head of the Shrikant Verma Trust, while promising to protect the rights of writers, is also a senior leader of a political party—the Shiv Sena (Shinde)—that keeps violating this very freedom of expression. We should not forget the attacks, criminal cases, and threats directed at comedian Kunal Kamra. It is because of the Shiv Sena (Shinde) that it has become impossible for Kamra to perform safely anywhere in India.

Nor should we forget the cancellation by SNDT University of a programme featuring historian Uma Chakravarti; the cancellation of Anand Teltumbde’s programme at the Kala Ghoda cultural festival; the cancellation of Naseeruddin Shah’s programme by Mumbai University; or the cases and arrests of students at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences. The Shinde-led Shiv Sena-BJP government has been responsible for these actions. The most recent instance is the inability to find a venue anywhere for the screening of a film about Umar Khalid. The Mumbai Police reportedly threatened every hall owner where the film might have been screened.

The party that is strangling a right that belongs to every citizen of India, but is as essential to a writer as oxygen—the right to freedom of expression—cannot, without irony, claim through a trust established by one of its senior leaders that it is committed to the welfare of writers and the advancement of literature.
It is rather like a murderer claiming that he is engaged in the noble work of ensuring the right to life. Is it civilised to listen to such a claim in silence?
Should the Shrikant Verma Trust be granted the right to speak on behalf of literature, or of writers, merely because the name Shrikant Verma is attached to it?

In another public statement, Verma said that no single ideology could claim ownership over a writer’s literature; literature is the common inheritance of humanity. He went on to say that the strength of Indian civilisation lies in dialogue among ideas, plurality of opinion, and coexistence, not in ideological segregation.

We do not know of any Indian civilisation whose strength has always lain in such coexistence. But the political alliance of which he is an important leader not only has little faith in the coexistence of different ideas; it has also repeatedly used the media, the mob, the police, and the law to suppress or eliminate dissenting views.

Where does any award ultimately derive its credibility or prestige? Suppose Donald Trump were to institute an award in Gandhi’s name tomorrow. Would we accept it? Would our respect for Gandhi be enough to make such an award legitimate?
The question for Ashok Vajpeyi

There can be no doubt that Ashok Vajpeyi is not someone who can be moved by the lure of money or an external honour. So what was it—his affection for Shrikantji—that compelled him to appear on the platform of a Trust run by a leader of a constituent of the BJP-led NDA, and by someone entrusted with the task of strengthening that political alliance?

Is the right that affection gives us necessarily reciprocal? Can Ashok Vajpeyi, by virtue of this affection, persuade the head of the Trust to distance himself from a politics that is, day after day, killing India? If this affection is not reciprocal, then what is the value of that affection?

But this is not only a question about Ashok Vajpeyi. There were many writers, artists, and cultural figures on the stage and in the auditorium who believe in the principle and practice of secularism. Were they there because of Shrikant Verma’s name? Or because of Ashok Vajpeyi’s?

One could argue that the programme, or the Trust, should not be linked to the politics of its members. But his public identity at present is inseparable from his politics. The Trust is being run with his resources. And he clearly wishes to strengthen his political identity. Social legitimacy is extremely useful for that purpose. A Trust such as this, and events of this kind, can serve that purpose.
Why power needs the writer

Interestingly, politicians are rarely satisfied with the power of politics alone. They need legitimacy from art and literature. Why did Indira Gandhi seek the support of writers during the Emergency? Did their proximity somehow add to her authority? Stalin, Mao, Hitler, or Narendra Modi—all have needed legitimacy from artists and writers. Modi needs Shah Rukh Khan, Aamir Khan. Why?

A writer has little else except the moral force, or aura, that literature gives him. There is perhaps only one thing he can do: deny this aura to a politics that is opposed to democracy. He has no weapon except non-cooperation.

Those who oppose democratic politics must be made to understand that they cannot expect any kind of proximity from us. Time and literature humanise people. The presence and companionship of artists and writers can also end up humanising those who are murderers of democracy.
If I am being honoured at the very moment when, because of your politics, someone from my own community is being arrested or killed, how am I supposed to face myself?

Every moment is not the same. The strange time that has fallen upon us like a shadow is one that perhaps no other generation in India has had to witness. Muslims are living without relief. Christians are living without relief. Democracy has been strangled.
Then why should we offer those practising the politics responsible for all this the comfort of our companionship?

Politics is always conducted by individuals. Why should we give those individuals the assurance that they can continue to practise a politics of hatred and violence in this country, and yet our affection will remain available to them whenever they want it?

Why can we not tell them that if they want our proximity, they will have to first distance themselves from the politics that has been thrust like a dagger into the heart of India? Is it too much to ask of ourselves?
Apoorvanand teaches Hindi at Delhi University and writes literary and cultural criticism.
